record.provider: Zenodo anonymous download throughput (the fetch-serving question)

free_tier.stated: Each record has a default storage quota of 50 GB, with an unlimited number of records under 50 GB, plus an additional allowance of up to 150 GB to distribute across uploads; no period is stated.
free_tier.notes: The 50 GB quota applies per record; the 150 GB is one total allowance assigned to records from the storage settings. The per-record cap, the request rate and the retention window are in limits[].

egress.terms: Free and unmetered, and HTTP Range (206) is supported anonymously, which is what makes the parallel read possible: 'accept-ranges: bytes', 'content-range: bytes 0-1023/81165133690'.

record.tooling: zenodo_get (pip) already parallelises; any HTTP client with range support (aria2c -x/-s, rclone non-backend http, curl --parallel) will do.
record.chaining: Per-connection shaping limits transfers to approximately 350-480 KB/s, requiring client-side concurrency rather than account multiplication. Measured throughput scaling: 1 connection yields 0.3 MB/s, 6 connections yield 2.33 MB/s, 16 connections yield 6.01 MB/s, 32 connections yield 11.95 MB/s, and 64 connections yield 23.07 MB/s. At 23 MB/s aggregate bandwidth delivers approximately 2 TB per day from a single host.

limits.value: 50 GB per record default; 200 GB absolute ceiling on a single record with the 150 GB allowance pooled in; max 100 files per record (new API: 'a limit of 50GB total in the record (and any given file), and up to 100 files in the record').

record.limits_note: Bandwidth shaping is enforced per TCP connection rather than per IP address. Sixty-four concurrent HTTP Range requests all returned HTTP 206 and aggregate throughput saturated local network capacity without an aggregate cap.

identity_cost.detail: inferred from the category 'academic'; the source record states no identity cost, so this is a class assumption, not evidence

record.reliability_note: Single-stream downloads are painfully slow (~215 KB/s on a 100MB range; the same range took 120s to deliver 45MB). Anything that does not parallelise will appear broken. Reading one file sequentially is a ~50x underuse of the link.
record.confidence_note: The read path and served byte count were measured on 2026-10-30 against published repository objects. Documented with supporting probe data.

card.summary: Each record comes with a default quota of 50 GB and an unlimited number of records may be uploaded under 50 GB; a further 150 GB additional allowance is held...

free_tier.stated: Each record comes with a default quota of 50 GB and an unlimited number of records may be uploaded under 50 GB; a further 150 GB additional allowance is held per account and can be distributed across records as needed.
free_tier.notes: CERN funds the service, so the quota is a policy that can move; it is not a purchased allowance with a contract behind it.

per_object_cap.notes: A record is the upload unit, not a file: up to 100 files may sit in one record, and their total volume may not exceed 50 GB.

retention.stated: Items are retained for the lifetime of the repository, currently the lifetime of the host laboratory CERN, whose experimental programme is defined for the next 20 years at least; a withdrawn record leaves a tombstone page and the DOI and URL of the original object are retained.
retention.notes: Permanence is the whole point of a DOI, and it is also why this is an archive rather than a working set.

egress.terms: free with no metered allowance; the published limits are on request count, not on transferred bytes: a guest may make 60 requests per minute, an authenticated user 100; files are served to an anonymous ranged GET without authentication.

record.interface_detail: REST deposit API with a token, plus an S3-compatible endpoint for large files. Not a WebDAV or rclone-native backend.
record.tooling: requests or curl against the deposit API; the S3 endpoint needs a generated key pair
record.chaining: The useful chain is write-once archive plus a parallel ranged reader: Zenodo holds the durable copy and a Worker or a ranged client serves it, because a single stream is slow but many streams are not.

limits.value: 50 GB per record, and 150 GB total per account
a DOI is minted on publish and the record is then immutable except for metadata; files may only be added in a 30-day window

record.limits_note: Two constraints bind: individual depositions are capped at 50 GB, and published records cannot be modified in place. Additional content requires creating new depositions with distinct DOIs.
record.binding_note: The cap is generous for the shard sizes; the gate is what decides the workflow, because a mistake after publication cannot be corrected in place, only superseded by a new version.

identity_cost.detail: A local account asks for a username, full name, affiliation, email address and password, and the email must be confirmed before the first upload; ORCID and GitHub logins are offered as alternatives and neither is required. No card and no institutional check.

record.reliability_note: CERN-operated and long-lived; the failure mode is policy change rather than downtime. Records are immutable after publication, so a quota reduction would affect new deposits and not existing ones. The binding limit on reading is the per-connection throttle, which parallel ranged GETs defeat; see zenodo-anonymous-download-throughput.
record.confidence_note: The quota and the write gate are read from CERN's own help pages on 2026-10-21; the throughput is measured separately in zenodo-anonymous-download-throughput.

card.provider: Zenodo DOI batching (automatic DataCite minting per record)
card.summary: One DOI per record, automatically, free, and unlimited records. DOI count is therefore not a constraint on sharding: a 410-record archive is also 410 citable...

record.provider: Zenodo DOI batching (automatic DataCite minting per record)

free_tier.stated: One DOI per record, automatically, free, and unlimited records. DOI count is therefore not a constraint on sharding: a 410-record archive is also 410 citable handles at no extra cost
free_tier.notes: Documents the Digital Object Identifier assignment mechanism for multi-part dataset partitioning.

per_object_cap.stated: One DOI per record, and the deposition response carries a reserved DOI already set through prereserve_doi, so a batch job gets a citable handle without a separate call

retention.stated: DOIs are permanent and cannot be reused or reassigned. Deleting a record within 30 days revokes the DOI, after which it tombstones. A record cannot be un-published to reclaim the identifier

egress.terms: Not applicable to the identifier itself. Retrieval of the deposited bytes is free and unmetered, and the read path is measured in the sibling record

record.interface_detail: POST /api/deposit/depositions returns a record with a reserved DOI already set, so one call per record yields one identifier
record.tooling: any HTTP client. zenodo_get and zenodo-cli both wrap the same API for the read side; there is no rclone backend
record.chaining: Because every record gets a DOI for free, a 410-record archive is also 410 citable handles with zero extra work. This is the mechanism that makes the unlimited-records story practical rather than merely permitted: there is no per-DOI cost and no approval step, so the archive can be sharded to the record boundary and every shard stays citable

limits.value: 100 requests per minute authenticated, 30 per minute on the search API, which sets the batch size per hour rather than any record count cap
a DOI is revoked if the record is deleted inside the 30-day window, and tombstones after that

record.binding_note: Nothing limits the number of DOIs. What limits a batch job is the authenticated request rate, so the practical ceiling is records per hour and not records per account
record.limits_note: Content outside the repository's scope is removed and its DOI revoked, which is the only stated ground for losing an identifier after the 30-day window

identity_cost.detail: an email address, GitHub or ORCID account. No institution is needed to mint a DOI, which is the unusual part

record.reliability_note: Batch-creating hundreds of records is API-rate-bound only and not quota-bound, so the operational risk is a batch that half-completes and leaves Pending files rather than one that hits a ceiling
record.confidence_note: What would raise it is a probe that creates a deposition anonymously or with a token and reads the reserved DOI back

evidence.proved: the quickstart creates a deposition, receives a 'doi' and 'prereserve_doi' in the response, uploads through a bucket URL, then POSTs to /publish, and notes the newer file API has 'a limit of 50GB total in the record (and any given file), and up to 100 files in the record'

'Content not considered to fall under the scope of the repository will be removed and associated DOIs issued by Zenodo revoked', and on withdrawal that the DOI and the URL of the original object are retained
deletion is owner-initiated within 30 days after publication; outside that window only justified cases are considered

record.notes: Zenodo dataset publishing assigns unique DOIs via DataCite. Individual datasets are capped at 50 GB per deposition, and automated DOI minting enables programmatic dataset sharding across multiple depositions.

extras.parent_finding: Zenodo's public deposit path at 50 GB per record times unlimited records
extras.what_the_parent_record_owns: the deposit API, the quota arithmetic, the 30-day window and the visibility model
extras.what_this_record_owns: that a DOI is minted per record at no cost, which is what allows the archive to be sharded to the record boundary without losing citability

record.provider: Zenodo restricted-access records and secret links (working storage, not only an archive)

free_tier.stated: The same 50 GB per record and 150 GB per-account pool as the public path. Restricting the files neither reduces nor refunds the quota, so the capacity is identical
free_tier.notes: Documents Zenodo restricted-access depositions and secret sharing links. Quota limits match standard public depositions with restricted visibility.

per_object_cap.stated: 50 GB per record on the default quota, with the 150 GB account pool distributable across records, and a hard 100 files per record
per_object_cap.notes: the 200 GB single-record figure is 50 GB plus the whole 150 GB pool, which requires distributing nothing else

retention.stated: A record cannot be deleted after 30 days. Restricted records carry the same rule, so a restricted record is as permanent as a public one and its quota is consumed monotonically

egress.terms: Free. A secret link grants 'Can view' on restricted or embargoed files of all current and future versions of that record, with optional expiry

record.interface_detail: the same deposition API; visibility is a field on the draft, set to restricted with an embargo date or a share link, and share links are managed from the record's Links tab
record.tooling: any HTTP client for the deposition and file APIs, working in the same way as the public path. There is no rclone backend, so uploads are plain HTTP PUT against a bucket URL
record.chaining: This is what turns Zenodo from a cold archive into something usable as a hot working set: data can be kept off the public index while still holding 50 GB times N, and still read it programmatically with a token or a shared link. It composes with the 32-connection parallel read measured on the public path, because the throttle is per connection and not per visibility

limits.value: 50 GB per record on the default quota, 100 files per record
a record cannot be deleted after 30 days, restricted or not
100 requests per minute authenticated; 30 per minute on the search API

record.binding_note: The quota and the visibility are independent, so restricting a record buys privacy and no capacity.
record.limits_note: Metadata is always public even when the files are restricted, so titles, descriptions and the minted DOI leak. That is a property of the visibility model and not a defect in this record

identity_cost.detail: an email address, GitHub or ORCID account. Restricting a record requires no additional verification.

record.reliability_note: Answers the working-storage question: workable for private data, but every record still carries permanently public metadata and a DOI, so it is a leaky private tier and not a private bucket. An interrupted upload leaves a Pending file that must be removed by hand
record.confidence_note: What would raise it is a probe of a restricted record read through a secret link

evidence.proved: 'Link sharing enables you to create a secret link which provides access to your record. The link can also have an expiry date.' and 'Can view: Grants access to view restricted/embargoed files of all current and future versions'
'the access right field has now been changed into a visibility field with two options (metadata is always public)'
each record comes with a default quota of 50 GB and an additional 150 GB allowance distributable across uploads, with no account-level total documented
records can be deleted by their owner within 30 days after publication, and outside that window only in justified cases

record.notes: Zenodo supports restricted-access records with secret sharing links alongside public records. Storage quota is 50 GB per deposition with identical API upload endpoints and lifecycle terms.
